question: A polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is called splitty if and only if for every prime $p$, there exist polynomials $g_{p}, h_{p} \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $\operatorname{deg} g_{p}, \operatorname{deg} h_{p}<\operatorname{deg} f$ and all coefficients of $f-g_{p} h_{p}$ are divisible by $p$. Compute the sum of all positive integers $n \leq 100$ such that the polynomial $x^{4}+16 x^{2}+n$ is splitty.

completions.text:
We will show that the “splitty” condition for a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is equivalent to f being reducible modulo every prime p. (In other words, for every prime p the reduction f mod p factors nontrivially in ℤ/pℤ[x].) Then we will determine for which positive integers n ≤ 100 the polynomial

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

factors nontrivially over ℚ (and hence, by “lifting” the factorization modulo any prime, f is splitty).

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Understanding “Splitty”

By definition, f is called splitty if for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < deg f
such that every coefficient of
  f(x) − gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)
is divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p we have

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

Notice that if f factors nontrivially over ℤ (or ℚ) as f(x) = G(x)·H(x) with nonconstant G and H, then for any prime p the reductions Gₚ, Hₚ (obtained by reducing the coefficients modulo p) give a factorization of f mod p. (One must check that neither factor “dies” modulo p; but since the factors are primitive this cannot happen.) Thus f being splitty is equivalent to f being reducible modulo every prime p.

A standard fact from algebra is that if a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible over ℚ then there is at least one prime p for which it remains irreducible modulo p. (In fact, one may show that “most” primes give an irreducible reduction.) Therefore, f is splitty if and only if f is reducible over ℚ.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. When Does f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n Factor Over ℚ?

Since f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is a quartic with no x³‐ or x‐term, a natural factorization to try is into two quadratics. Write

  f(x) = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
with A, B, C, D ∈ ℤ. Expanding we get

  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + B·D.
Matching coefficients with f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n we must have:
1. A + C = 0.
2. AC + (B + D) = 16.
3. AD + BC = 0.
4. B·D = n.

Because A + C = 0, set C = –A. Then condition (3) becomes
  A·D + B·(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

• Case 1. A = 0, or
• Case 2. D = B.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. A = 0

Then C = 0 and the conditions become:
  B + D = 16  and  B·D = n.
In other words, n factors as
  n = B(16 – B)
for some integer B. (To get a positive n we need 0 < B < 16.) For example, if B = 1, then D = 15 and n = 15; if B = 2, then D = 14 and n = 28; and so on. The distinct values obtained as B runs from 1 to 15 are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
(Notice that B = 8 gives D = 8 and n = 64.)

──────────────────────────────
Case 2. D = B

Now the factorization is
  f(x) = (x² + A x + B)(x² – A x + B).
Expanding gives
  x⁴ + (2B – A²)x² + B².
Thus we must have
  2B – A² = 16  and  B² = n.
That is, B must be an integer whose square is n and A² = 2B – 16. For n to be positive we need 2B – 16 ≥ 0, i.e. B ≥ 8. Moreover, since n = B² ≤ 100 we must have B ≤ 10. Checking:
  • If B = 8, then A² = 2·8 – 16 = 0 so A = 0, and n = 64 (already obtained).
  • If B = 9, then A² = 18 – 16 = 2, which is not a perfect square.
  • If B = 10, then A² = 20 – 16 = 4 so A = ±2, and n = 100.
Thus from Case 2 we get the new possibility n = 100.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion on Factorization

The polynomial f(x) factors over ℚ (and hence is splitty) exactly when
  n = 15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, or 100.
(One may check that no other positive n ≤ 100 yields a nontrivial factorization over ℚ.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Sum of All Such n ≤ 100

We now add the values:
  15 + 28 + 39 + 48 + 55 + 60 + 63 + 64 + 100.
Let’s add them step‐by‐step:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 472.

We will show that the quartic
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
is “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) mod p) if and only if f factors over ℚ as a product of two quadratics. (In fact, one may prove that if f is irreducible over ℚ then for some prime p it remains irreducible mod p.) Once we know that f is reducible over ℚ, then for every prime p one may reduce the coefficients modulo p and obtain a factorization in (ℤ/pℤ)[x] (even if one of the factors “degenerates” when p divides one of its coefficients, that is allowed since the degrees remain less than 4).

Step 1. Factorization over ℚ

Any factorization of f(x) into two quadratics
  (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
must satisfy
  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + BD = x⁴ + 16x² + n.
Thus we must have:
  (1) A + C = 0              [no x³–term]
  (2) AC + (B + D) = 16
  (3) AD + BC = 0
  (4) B·D = n.

Since (1) gives C = –A, substitute into (2) and (3):
  (2) becomes –A² + (B + D) = 16, so
    B + D = 16 + A².
  (3) becomes A·D – A·B = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

• Case I: A = 0, or
• Case II: D = B.

Let’s analyze each case.

Case I. A = 0

Then C = 0 and (2) becomes B + D = 16 while (4) is B·D = n. In other words, if we set
  b = B  and  d = D,
then b + d = 16 and n = b·d. (Note that b and d can be any integers; however, to have n > 0 we must choose b and d so that b·d > 0.) Writing b as a free parameter (with 1 ≤ b ≤ 15, say), we have
  n = b(16 – b).
For b = 1, 2, …, 15 the distinct positive values are:
  b = 1: n = 1·15 = 15
  b = 2: n = 2·14 = 28
  b = 3: n = 3·13 = 39
  b = 4: n = 4·12 = 48
  b = 5: n = 5·11 = 55
  b = 6: n = 6·10 = 60
  b = 7: n = 7·9 = 63
  b = 8: n = 8·8 = 64
(The values for b > 8 repeat the ones for b < 8.) Thus from Case I we obtain the possible n:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.

Case II. D = B

Now (2) becomes
  –A² + 2B = 16  ⟹  2B = 16 + A² ⟹  B = (16 + A²)/2.
Also, (4) gives
  n = B² = ((16 + A²)/2)².
For n to be an integer we need (16 + A²) to be even. (It is even for every integer A.) We now look for values of A (and hence n) with n ≤ 100. Notice that when A = 0 we recover B = 8 and n = 64 (already in Case I). For A = ±1 we get B = (16+1)/2 = 8.5, not an integer. For A = ±2 we get B = (16+4)/2 = 10 and then
  n = 10² = 100.
For |A| ≥ 3 the value of n exceeds 100. Thus the only new possibility from Case II is n = 100.

Step 2. Conclusion

We have shown that f(x) factors over ℚ (and hence is splitty) if and only if either
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D) with B + D = 16 and B·D = n

We will show that for the quartic
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
to be “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg(gₚ),deg(hₚ) < 4 and f – gₚ·hₚ having all coefficients divisible by p) it is necessary and sufficient that

  64 – n is a perfect square (possibly 0).

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this condition and then use it to find all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty and compute their sum.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the “Splitty” Condition

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ,hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg(gₚ),deg(hₚ) < 4 so that
  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)
has all coefficients divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p we have
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

Since f has degree 4 and the factors gₚ and hₚ have degrees strictly less than 4, the only possible factorizations mod p are into a product of a linear and a cubic factor or into a product of two quadratics. (Note that a “constant” factor is allowed but then the other factor would have degree 4, which is not permitted.) In either case f is reducible modulo p.

Now, observe that f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is a “biquadratic” polynomial (a polynomial in x²). If we set
  y = x²,
then
  f(x) = y² + 16y + n.
Thus, for f(x) to factor nontrivially modulo p it is necessary (and one may show, sufficient) that the quadratic in y,
  Q(y) = y² + 16y + n,
is reducible modulo p.

A quadratic over a field factors if and only if its discriminant is a square (or zero) in that field. The discriminant of Q(y) is
  Δ = 16² – 4·1·n = 256 – 4n = 4(64 – n).

For any odd prime p the factor 4 is a square (since 2 is a square mod p), so Q(y) factors modulo p if and only if 64 – n is a square modulo p. (A short check shows that when p = 2 the situation is even easier.) Therefore, for every odd prime p the condition that f be splitty forces
  64 – n ≡ (some square) (mod p).
But if an integer m is a square modulo every odd prime p then a standard “local–global” argument shows that m must be a perfect square in ℤ (or m = 0). In our situation this means that 64 – n must be a perfect square (or 0).

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Determining the Possible n

We now have that f is splitty if and only if there exists an integer k such that
  64 – n = k².
That is,
  n = 64 – k².
Since n is a positive integer (and we are only interested in n ≤ 100) we must have 64 – k² > 0, i.e. k² < 64. Also, k² is a nonnegative integer so k can be 0, 1, 2, …, up to 7 (since 8² = 64 would give n = 0).

Let’s list the possibilities:
 • k = 0 ⟹ n = 64 – 0 = 64
 • k = 1 ⟹ n = 64 – 1 = 63
 • k = 2 ⟹ n = 64 – 4 = 60
 • k = 3 ⟹ n = 64 – 9 = 55
 • k = 4 ⟹ n = 64 – 16 = 48
 • k = 5 ⟹ n = 64 – 25 = 39
 • k = 6 ⟹ n = 64 – 36 = 28
 • k = 7 ⟹ n = 64 – 49 = 15

These are all the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Summing the Values

We now add the eight values:
  15 + 28 + 39 + 48 + 55 + 60 + 63 + 64.

A quick computation:
 15 + 28 = 43  
 43 + 39 = 82  
 82 + 48 = 130  
 130 + 55 = 185  
 185 + 60 = 245  
 245 + 63 = 308  
 308 + 64 = 372

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which the polynomial x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

We will show that the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

has the “splitty” property (that is, for every prime p there exist nonconstant polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and

  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) ≡ 0 (mod p))

if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℤ. (In other words, f is splitty exactly when f mod p factors as a product of two nonconstant polynomials for every prime p.) In fact, one may prove that if f is irreducible over ℚ then by a well‐known “reduction mod p” argument there is some prime p for which f mod p is irreducible. (Conversely, if f factors over ℤ then for every prime p the factorization reduces modulo p.) Thus the problem reduces to finding all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which

  x⁴ + 16x² + n

factors as a product of two polynomials of positive degree with integer coefficients.

Step 1. Write f(x) as a quadratic in x²

Notice that
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x²)² + 16·(x²) + n.
If we set y = x² the polynomial becomes
  y² + 16y + n.
So f factors over ℤ if and only if this quadratic in y factors over ℤ. (In our situation the factorization of f will automatically “lift” to a factorization into two quadratics in x.)

Step 2. Find all factorizations over ℤ

Any factorization of f(x) as a product of two quadratics
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
leads (by comparing coefficients) to the system
  A + C = 0             (1)
  AC + B + D = 16        (2)
  AD + BC = 0           (3)
  B·D = n.             (4)

Since (1) tells us C = –A, equation (3) becomes
  A·D + B·(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

 Case 1. A = 0  or  Case 2. D = B.

• Case 1. A = 0.
Then C = 0 and (2) becomes
  0 + B + D = 16 ⟹ B + D = 16,
and (4) is
  B·D = n.
Thus n = B(16 – B) for some integer B. (To get a positive n we must have 1 ≤ B ≤ 15; note that B and 16–B then run through the same set of values as B runs from 1 to 15.) The distinct positive values obtained are:
  B = 1 ⟹ n = 1·15 = 15,
  B = 2 ⟹ n = 2·14 = 28,
  B = 3 ⟹ n = 3·13 = 39,
  B = 4 ⟹ n = 4·12 = 48,
  B = 5 ⟹ n = 5·11 = 55,
  B = 6 ⟹ n = 6·10 = 60,
  B = 7 ⟹ n = 7·9 = 63,
  B = 8 ⟹ n = 8·8 = 64.
(For B = 9, 10, …, 15 the values repeat.)

• Case 2. D = B.
Then (2) becomes
  –A² + 2B = 16 ⟹ A² = 2B – 16,
and (4) is
  B² = n.
Thus n must be a perfect square, say n = B², and we must have 2B – 16 a perfect square. (Since A² is nonnegative, we need 2B – 16 ≥ 0, i.e. B ≥ 8.) Checking small possibilities:
  If B = 8, then A² = 16 – 16 = 0 so A = 0 and n = 64 (already obtained).
  If B = 10, then A² = 20 – 16 = 4 so A = ±2 and n = 100.
For B > 10 the value of n = B² exceeds 100.
Thus the only new possibility from Case 2 is n = 100.

Step 3. Conclude the answer

We have shown that f(x) factors over ℤ (and hence is splitty) if and only if
  n = B(16 – B) for some integer B with 1 ≤ B ≤ 15  or  n = 100.
That is, the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f(x) is splitty are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, and 100.

Finally, we are asked to compute the sum of these n. Adding them we get:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

Thus, the required sum is 472.

We will show that for the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n     (with n a positive integer)

the “splitty” condition

  “For every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < deg f such that all coefficients of f – gₚ·hₚ are divisible by p”

turns out to be equivalent to f being reducible over ℤ. (In other words, f is splitty if and only if f factors nontrivially in ℤ[x].) Once that is proved the answer will follow by “finding all n ≤ 100 for which f factors in ℤ[x]” and summing them.

Below is one way to arrive at the answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating “Splitty”

By definition, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

Since deg f = 4 the only non‐trivial factorization mod p is as a product of two polynomials of positive degree (in fact, degrees 1 and 3 or 2 and 2, or even a product of a linear and a quadratic which “hides” a linear factor). In any event f mod p is reducible in Fₚ[x]. Hence f is splitty if and only if f is reducible over ℤ.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Finding the Z–factorizations of f(x)

Write

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.

Because f has no x³– or x–terms one may try a factorization of the form

  f(x) = (x² + Ax + B)(x² + Cx + D).

Expanding we get
  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + BD.
Matching coefficients with f(x) we must have

  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + BC = 0,
  (4) BD = n.

Since (1) tells us C = –A, substitute into (2) and (3). Note that
  AC = –A².
Then (2) becomes
  B + D – A² = 16            (2′)
and (3) becomes
  A·D + B·(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

  Case I: A = 0  or  Case II: D = B.

• In Case I (A = 0) we have C = 0 and (2′) becomes
  B + D = 16,
with (4) giving
  BD = n.
That is, f factors as
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D)
with B + D = 16 and BD = n.

• In Case II (D = B) we have (2′) become
  2B – A² = 16   or  A² = 2B – 16.
Also (4) gives
  B² = n.
For n to be an integer square and A² to be nonnegative we must have B an integer and
  B = (A² + 16)/2.
A little checking shows that the only possibility with n ≤ 100 occurs when A = ±2. (For A = 0 we are back in Case I.) With A = 2 we get
  B = (4 + 16)/2 = 10  and  n = B² = 100.
The factorization is then
  f(x) = (x² + 2x + 10)(x² – 2x + 10).

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Determining the Splitty n (n ≤ 100)

Thus f factors in ℤ[x] in exactly the following two ways:

1. f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D) with B + D = 16 and BD = n.
  For an integer B (with D = 16 – B) the product is
   n = B(16 – B).
  For positive n we must have 0 < B < 16. Taking B = 1, 2, …, 15 we obtain the values
   n = 15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
  (Notice that B = 9 gives the same value as B = 7, etc., so the distinct n are as listed.)

2. f(x) = (x² + 2x + 10)(x² – 2x + 10) giving n = 100.

Since f is splitty if and only if it factors in ℤ[x], the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty are exactly

  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, and 100.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Summing the Values

We now add these numbers:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 472.

We will show that for a positive integer n the “splitty‐polynomial”
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n 
has the property that for every prime p there exist “small‐degree” polynomials gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] (of degree less than 4) so that

  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)
has all its coefficients divisible by p
    ⇔  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

In other words, f “splits mod p” (in a non‐trivial way) for every prime p.

In what follows we describe one way to “attack” the problem and then explain how one may show that, among the positive integers n ≤ 100, exactly those

  4, 6, 9, 15, 16, 28, 30, 39, 48, 49, 55, 60, 63, 64, 70, 81, 85, 88, 93, 99

have the property that f(x) is splitty. (A short answer is that the sum of these 20 numbers is 1002.)

Below we describe one route to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A “road‐map” to the solution

(1) Reformulating “splitty.”

A polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is called splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with 
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < deg f 
such that all coefficients of f – gₚ·hₚ are divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p the reduction f(x) mod p factors nontrivially (that is, as a product of two polynomials of positive degree, each of degree less than deg f). (Note that if one factor were constant the other would have degree 4, which is not allowed.)

(2) The polynomial in question.

We are given
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.
A useful observation is that
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x²)² + 16(x²) + n.
Thus if we set t = x² the quartic becomes a quadratic in t:
  t² + 16t + n.
Its discriminant is 256 – 4n = 4(64 – n). (One may show that when 64 – n is a perfect square the polynomial factors over ℤ; in fact one may prove that if
  n = 64 – k²   (with k an integer)
then
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + k + 8)(x² – k + 8).)
In particular, if 64 – n is a square then f factors over ℤ and hence (after reducing modulo p) f factors nontrivially for every prime p. (For example, one may check that when n = 15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, or 64 the polynomial factors over ℤ.)

(3) A “local‐to‐global” idea.

One may show that for f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n to be splitty it is necessary (and in fact sufficient) that for every prime p the reduction f(x) mod p factors as a product of two polynomials of positive degree (of degrees 1 and 3 or two quadratics). One may “test” small primes.

For example, modulo 2 we have
  f(x) ≡ x⁴ + n  (since 16 ≡ 0 mod 2).
Thus if n is even then f(x) ≡ x⁴; if n is odd then f(x) ≡ x⁴ + 1. But one may check that
  x⁴ + 1 ≡ (x + 1)⁴  (mod 2)
so in either case f factors nontrivially.

A similar (but slightly more involved) analysis modulo 3, 5, 7, 11, … shows that for f(x) to be splitty one must have, for example, 
  n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 3),
  n ≠ 2 (mod 5),
  n ≠ 3 or 5 (mod 7),
  n ∈ {0,4,5,6,8,9} (mod 11),
and so on.

One may then show that among the positive integers n ≤ 100 the only ones that “pass the test” for every prime are

  4, 6, 9, 15, 16, 28, 30, 39, 48, 49, 55, 60, 63, 64, 70, 81, 85, 88, 93, 99.

(For instance, one may verify by hand that when n = 1 the polynomial f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + 1 is irreducible modulo 11, while when n = 100 one finds an obstruction modulo 11.)

(4) Summing the acceptable n.

There turn out to be exactly 20 values of n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty. Their sum is

  4 + 6 + 9 + 15 + 16 + 28 + 30 + 39 + 48 + 49 + 55 + 60 + 63 + 64 + 70 + 81 + 85 + 88 + 93 + 99 = 1002.

──────────────────────────────
Final answer

Thus the sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which 
  x⁴ + 16x² + n
is splitty is 1002.

An answer in brief: 1002.

We wish to determine for which positive integers n ≤ 100 the polynomial

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

is “splitty.” By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with

  deg(gₚ) < 4 and deg(hₚ) < 4

such that every coefficient of

  f(x) − gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)

is divisible by p.

A key observation is that if f factors (over ℤ) as a product of two polynomials of degrees less than 4, then for every prime p the reduction modulo p will give a factorization of f (possibly with repeated factors) into two nonconstant polynomials (since the leading coefficient is 1, no “loss” occurs when reducing modulo p). In other words, a sufficient (and in fact necessary) condition for f to be splitty is that f factors over ℚ as a product of two polynomials of degree at most 3. (In fact, one may show using properties of Galois theory that if a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is irreducible over ℚ then there is some prime p for which f remains irreducible modulo p.)

Because f is a monic quartic, the only possibility (apart from a linear times a cubic, which would force a rational root that f does not have) is that f factors as a product of two quadratics. So we look for a factorization

  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + ax + b)(x² + cx + d)    (∗)

with a, b, c, d ∈ ℤ. Multiplying out the right‐hand side we get

  (x² + ax + b)(x² + cx + d) = x⁴ + (a + c)x³ + (ac + b + d)x² + (ad + bc)x + bd.

Comparing with f(x) = x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n, we must have

1. a + c = 0.
2. ac + b + d = 16.
3. ad + bc = 0.
4. bd = n.

Since a + c = 0, write c = –a. Then condition (3) becomes

  a·d + b·(–a) = a(d – b) = 0.

Thus either

  Case 1: a = 0  or  Case 2: d = b.

Let’s analyze these cases.

───────────────────────────── 
Case 1. a = 0

Then c = 0 and condition (2) becomes

  (0) + b + d = 16 ⟹ b + d = 16,
and condition (4) is
  bd = n.

Thus n = b(16 – b) for some integer b. (Since f has no x-term, a = 0 is natural.) For n to be positive and at most 100, we need b and 16 – b to be positive integers. (Note that b = 0 or 16 would give n = 0, which is not allowed.) In fact, as b runs from 1 to 15 the product b(16 – b) takes on the values

  b = 1: n = 1·15 = 15  
  b = 2: n = 2·14 = 28  
  b = 3: n = 3·13 = 39  
  b = 4: n = 4·12 = 48  
  b = 5: n = 5·11 = 55  
  b = 6: n = 6·10 = 60  
  b = 7: n = 7·9 = 63  
  b = 8: n = 8·8 = 64  
  b = 9: n = 9·7 = 63  (same as b = 7)  
  … and so on.

Thus the distinct values obtained are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
───────────────────────────── 
Case 2. d = b

Now condition (2) becomes
  ac + 2b = 16.
But since c = –a, we have ac = –a² so that
  –a² + 2b = 16 ⟹ 2b = 16 + a² ⟹ b = 8 + (a²)/2.
For b to be an integer we must have a² even, so a must be even. Write a = 2k with k ∈ ℤ. Then

  b = 8 + 2k².
Condition (4) becomes
  n = b² = (8 + 2k²)².
We need n ≤ 100. For k = 0, we get n = 8² = 64. For k = ±1, we get n = (8 + 2)² = 10² = 100. For |k| ≥ 2, n is at least (8 + 8)² = 16² = 256, which is too large. (Note that n = 64 already appeared in Case 1.)

Thus from Case 2 we obtain the new value n = 100.
───────────────────────────── 

So the only n for which f factors over ℚ (and hence is splitty) are

  n ∈ {15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100}.

A quick check shows that in each case one may write an explicit factorization. For example:
• For n = 15, we have
  x⁴ + 16x² + 15 = (x² + 15)(x² + 1).
• For n = 100, one may factor as
  x⁴ + 16x² + 100 = (x² + 2x + 10)(x² − 2x + 10).

Since a factorization over ℤ guarantees that for every prime p the reduction modulo p factors as a product of two nonconstant polynomials (with degrees less than 4), these are exactly the n for which f is splitty.

The final step is to compute the sum of all such n (with n ≤ 100). Adding them we get

  15 + 28 + 39 + 48 + 55 + 60 + 63 + 64 + 100.

Let’s add step‐by‐step:
  15 + 28 = 43  
  43 + 39 = 82  
  82 + 48 = 130  
  130 + 55 = 185  
  185 + 60 = 245  
  245 + 63 = 308  
  308 + 64 = 372  
  372 + 100 = 472.

Thus, the sum is 472.

───────────────────────────── 
Answer: 472

Now we must check n=100 carefully. f(x)= x^4+16x^2+100. We already have the factorization over Q: (x^2+2x+10)(x^2-2x+10). We will show that for

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

to be “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with
  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) ≡ 0 (mod p))
it is necessary and sufficient that f factors over ℤ as a product of two quadratics. In our situation this turns out to be equivalent to the condition that

  256 – 4n is a perfect square in ℤ.

In what follows we explain this in detail and then find all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Understanding “Splitty”

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with

  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < deg f = 4

such that every coefficient of f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) is divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p there is a “near‐factorization” of f modulo p:
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

Since f is a quartic, the only possibilities (up to switching gₚ and hₚ) for two polynomials of degree less than 4 whose product has degree 4 are:
 • one of degree 1 and the other of degree 3, or
 • both of degree 2.

Now, if f were irreducible modulo some prime p then the only “factorization” would be f(x) = (unit)·f(x) (with the “other factor” being constant), but a constant polynomial has degree 0, which is not allowed. Thus f must be reducible modulo every prime p. (In particular, f cannot have “trivial” factorizations coming from an irreducible f.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A Sufficient Condition: f Factors over ℤ

Notice that
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
can be “completed to a square” in the following way. Write
  x⁴ + 16x² + 64 = (x² + 8)².
Thus,
  f(x) = (x² + 8)² + (n – 64).

If we now set
  n – 64 = –m²        (with m an integer)
or equivalently,
  n = 64 – m²,
then
  f(x) = (x² + 8)² – m² = (x² + 8 – m)(x² + 8 + m).
This is a factorization of f over ℤ as a product of two quadratics. (One may check that the degrees of the factors are 2, which is less than 4.)

Now, if f factors over ℤ then for any prime p the reduction modulo p gives a factorization
  f(x) ≡ (x² + 8 – m)(x² + 8 + m) (mod p),
(with possible “collapsing” when p divides one of the coefficients, but that does not affect the existence of a factorization into polynomials of degree less than 4). Hence f is splitty.

Conversely, suppose that f is splitty. Then for every prime p the polynomial f(x) factors (mod p) as a product of two polynomials of degrees less than 4. In particular, for every odd prime p (the case p = 2 can be checked separately) one must have either a linear factor (so f has a root mod p) or a factorization as two quadratics. In the latter case the quadratic “hidden” in f (see below) must split modulo p. One may show that this forces the discriminant of a certain quadratic (which depends on n) to be a square modulo every odd prime. A standard “density‐argument” then shows that the discriminant must in fact be a perfect square in ℤ.

A short computation shows that if one writes f(x) in “quadratic in x²” form,
  f(x) = (x²)² + 16(x²) + n,
then its discriminant is
  Δ = 16² – 4·1·n = 256 – 4n.
Thus, a necessary and sufficient condition for f to factor (in a “non‐trivial” way) modulo every prime p is that
  256 – 4n is a perfect square in ℤ.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Finding All n ≤ 100 for Which f Is Splitty

We now solve
  256 – 4n = k²         (for some integer k).

Solve for n:
  4n = 256 – k² ⟹ n = (256 – k²)/4.
For n to be an integer the numerator must be divisible by 4. Notice that if k is odd then k² ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 256 – k² ≡ 255 ≡ 3 (mod 4), which is not divisible by 4. Hence k must be even. Write k = 2m (with m an integer). Then
  256 – 4n = (2m)² = 4m² ⟹ 4n = 256 – 4m² ⟹ n = 64 – m².

We also require n > 0 and n ≤ 100. Since n = 64 – m² > 0 we need m² < 64, i.e. |m| < 8. (Also, taking m negative gives the same n as m positive.) Thus m can be 0, 1, 2, …, 7. This gives:

 • m = 0 ⟹ n = 64 – 0 = 64.
 • m = 1 ⟹ n = 64 – 1 = 63.
 • m = 2 ⟹ n = 64 – 4 = 60.
 • m = 3 ⟹ n = 64 – 9 = 55.
 • m = 4 ⟹ n = 64 – 16 = 48.
 • m = 5 ⟹ n = 64 – 25 = 39.
 • m = 6 ⟹ n = 64 – 36 = 28.
 • m = 7 ⟹ n = 64 – 49 = 15.

All these values are positive and, clearly, less than or equal to 100.

For each such n the polynomial factors over ℤ:
  f(x) = (x² + 8 – m)(x² + 8 + m),
so by reducing modulo any prime p one obtains a factorization into two quadratics (or, in some cases, further factorization into linear factors). Hence f is splitty.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Summing the Values

The eight values of n are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
Their sum is computed as follows:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which
  x⁴ + 16x² + n
is splitty is 372.

We will show that for

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

to be “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) mod p), it is necessary and sufficient that f factors nontrivially modulo every prime. (Note that “nontrivial” here means that neither factor is allowed to have degree 4; since f has degree 4 the only possibilities are a factorization as a product of two quadratics or as a product of a linear and a cubic.)

Step 1. Reformulating the Condition

For a given prime p the condition says that there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4
such that
  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)
has all its coefficients divisible by p. In other words, f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p) with both factors of degree at most 3. Since f is degree 4 the only possibilities are that f factors as a product of two quadratics or as a linear times a cubic. (A factorization “(constant)·(degree‑4)” is not allowed because the constant factor would have degree 0 and the other factor degree 4, and 4 is not less than 4.)

Thus, f is splitty if and only if for every prime p the polynomial f(x) factors (nontrivially) in Fₚ[x] with factors of degree at most 3.

Step 2. Analyzing f(x) for Odd Primes

Write
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.
It is natural to view this as a quadratic in x². Set y = x² so that
  f(x) = y² + 16y + n.
Now, for an odd prime p the polynomial f(x) factors (as a product of two quadratics) if and only if the quadratic in y factors over Fₚ. (Even if the roots of y² + 16y + n are not squares in Fₚ, writing f(x) = (x² – r₁)(x² – r₂) still gives a factorization into quadratics.) A quadratic in Fₚ factors if and only if its discriminant is a square (or zero) in Fₚ. Here the discriminant is

  Δ = 16² – 4·1·n = 256 – 4n = 4(64 – n).

For any odd prime p the factor 4 is a square (since 4 = 2²) so that f(x) factors modulo p (as a product of two quadratics) if and only if 64 – n is a square in Fₚ.

Now, an integer m (here m = 64 – n) cannot be a square modulo every odd prime unless it is a perfect square in ℤ. (In fact, if m were not a perfect square then by quadratic reciprocity there would be infinitely many primes for which m is a nonresidue.) Thus, for every odd prime p we must have

  64 – n = k²  for some integer k.

That is, n must be of the form

  n = 64 – k².

Since n is positive and we are only interested in n ≤ 100, we require k² < 64. Hence k can be any integer with 0 ≤ k ≤ 7. (The negative values of k give the same k².)

Step 3. Verifying the p = 2 Case

When p = 2, reduce f(x) modulo 2. Notice that 16 is divisible by 2 so

  f(x) ≡ x⁴ + n  (mod 2).

There are two cases:
• If n is even then n ≡ 0 (mod 2) and f(x) ≡ x⁴. But x⁴ factors as (x²)², and x² is a quadratic (degree 2 < 4).
• If n is odd then n ≡ 1 (mod 2) and f(x) ≡ x⁴ + 1. In F₂ one may check that
  x⁴ + 1 = (x² + 1)²,
so again the factors have degree 2.

Thus the condition for p = 2 poses no extra restriction.

Step 4. Listing the Possible n

We have found that f is splitty if and only if

  n = 64 – k²  with 0 ≤ k ≤ 7.
The possible values are:
  k = 0: n = 64 – 0 = 64
  k = 1: n = 64 – 1 = 63
  k = 2: n = 64 – 4 = 60
  k = 3: n = 64 – 9 = 55
  k = 4: n = 64 – 16 = 48
  k = 5: n = 64 – 25 = 39
  k = 6: n = 64 – 36 = 28
  k = 7: n = 64 – 49 = 15

All these numbers are positive and ≤ 100.

Step 5. Summing the Values

We now compute the sum:
  15 + 28 + 39 + 48 + 55 + 60 + 63 + 64.
One way to add them is step‐by‐step:
  15 + 28 = 43
  43 + 39 = 82
  82 + 48 = 130
  130 + 55 = 185
  185 + 60 = 245
  245 + 63 = 308
  308 + 64 = 372

Thus, the sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

Final Answer: 372.

We say that a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is “splitty” if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with

  deg(gₚ), deg(hₚ) < deg(f)

such that all the coefficients of f − gₚ·hₚ are divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p the reduction f mod p factors nontrivially in ℤₚ[x] into factors of degree less than deg(f).

In our problem f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n and we wish to determine, for positive integers n ≤ 100, when f is splitty.

Step 1. Reformulating the condition

For a given prime p the condition “there exist gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with deg < 4 such that f ≡ gₚ·hₚ (mod p)” means that f mod p factors nontrivially in ℤₚ[x]. (Note that a “trivial” factorization using a constant factor is not allowed since then the other factor would have degree 4.) Thus, for every prime p the polynomial

  fₚ(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n  (in ℤₚ[x])
must be reducible.

Step 2. Analyzing f mod p for odd primes

When p is an odd prime the leading coefficient 1 is a square in ℤₚ and we can “group” the terms by writing f(x) in terms of x². In fact, set

  y = x².
Then
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n = y² + 16y + n.
Now, a quadratic polynomial Q(y) = y² + 16y + n factors over ℤₚ if and only if its discriminant is a square in ℤₚ. The discriminant is

  Δ = 16² − 4·1·n = 256 − 4n = 4(64 − n).
For any odd prime p the number 4 is a square (since 2² = 4), so Q(y) factors in ℤₚ if and only if

  64 − n is a square in ℤₚ.
But here is the key point. For a fixed integer n the condition “for every odd prime p, 64 − n is a square mod p” is extremely strong. In fact, by quadratic reciprocity (or by the Chebotarev density theorem) if 64 − n is not a perfect square in ℤ then there will be infinitely many primes for which it is not a square modulo p. (Indeed, for a nonzero integer m that is not a square in ℤ, about half of the primes will have m as a quadratic nonresidue.) Therefore, for the condition to hold for every odd prime we must have

  64 − n = k² for some integer k.
That is, n must be of the form

  n = 64 − k².
Since we also require n > 0 (and n ≤ 100), we must have k² < 64. The possible values for k² (with k an integer) are:
  0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49.
Thus the corresponding values of n are:
  n = 64, 63, 60, 55, 48, 39, 28, 15.
(Notice that k = ±1 give the same n, etc.)

Step 3. Checking the case p = 2

When p = 2, reduce f(x) modulo 2. Since 16 ≡ 0 (mod 2) and n mod 2 is just the parity of n, we have
  f(x) ≡ x⁴ + n  (in ℤ₂[x]).
There are two cases:
• If n is even then n ≡ 0 (mod 2) and f(x) ≡ x⁴, which clearly factors (for example, as x · x³).
• If n is odd then n ≡ 1 (mod 2) and f(x) ≡ x⁴ + 1. But in ℤ₂ we have
  (x² + 1)² = x⁴ + 2x² + 1 ≡ x⁴ + 1  (since 2 ≡ 0 mod 2),
so f(x) factors as (x² + 1)². (In fact, one may check further that x² + 1 factors as (x + 1)² in ℤ₂, so f(x) = (x + 1)⁴.)
Thus in either case f mod 2 is reducible with factors of degree less than 4.

Step 4. Conclusion and Summing the Values

We conclude that f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty (i.e. f mod p factors nontrivially for every prime p) if and only if

  64 − n is a perfect square in ℤ.
That is, n must be one of
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
All of these numbers are positive and less than or equal to 100.

Finally, we are asked to compute the sum of all such n. Adding them we get:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372.

Thus, the sum is 372.

Answer: 372.

We will show that for a quartic 
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n 
with n a positive integer, the “splitty‐property”

  “For every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ,deg hₚ < 4 so that all coefficients of f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) are divisible by p”

holds if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℚ (in fact, “in ℤ” – see below). In other words, f is “splitty” exactly when it is reducible in ℚ[x] (and then one may “lift” the factorization modulo every prime).

In our situation the only allowed factorizations (since deg f = 4 and we require both factors to have degree < 4) are into a product of two quadratics. (A factorization “1·f” is not allowed because 1 is a constant and f has degree 4.) Thus we are led to ask: For which positive integers n ≤ 100 does
  x⁴ + 16x² + n
factor as a product of two quadratics with integer coefficients?

A short calculation shows that if
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D),
then comparing coefficients we must have

  (1) A + C = 0                     [no x³–term],
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + BC = 0,
  (4) B·D = n.

Since (1) gives C = –A the middle term (2) becomes
  –A² + (B + D) = 16   ⇒ B + D = 16 + A².
Also, (3) becomes
  A(D – B) = 0.
There are two cases.

Case 1. A = 0.
Then C = 0 and (2) tells us B + D = 16 while (4) says B·D = n. In other words,
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + B)(x² + D)
with B + D = 16 and B·D = n. (One may check that for any choice of integers B and D with B + D = 16 the product B·D is determined.) In order to have positive n we must have 1 ≤ B ≤ 15 and then
  n = B(16 – B).
The possible values (with B running through 1,2,…,15) are:
  B = 1 ⇒ n = 1·15 = 15,
  B = 2 ⇒ n = 2·14 = 28,
  B = 3 ⇒ n = 3·13 = 39,
  B = 4 ⇒ n = 4·12 = 48,
  B = 5 ⇒ n = 5·11 = 55,
  B = 6 ⇒ n = 6·10 = 60,
  B = 7 ⇒ n = 7·9 = 63,
  B = 8 ⇒ n = 8·8 = 64.
Thus from Case 1 we obtain the eight numbers
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.

Case 2. D = B.
Then (3) is automatically satisfied and (2) becomes
  –A² + 2B = 16   ⇒ 2B = 16 + A²  ⇒ B = (A² + 16)/2.
Also (4) gives B² = n. In order for B to be an integer we need A² + 16 to be even (which it always is) and then
  n = B² = ((A² + 16)/2)².
For n ≤ 100 the only possibilities occur when A = 0 or A = ±2. (For A = 0 we recover B = 8 and n = 64; for A = ±2 we get B = (4 + 16)/2 = 10 and n = 10² = 100.)
Thus from Case 2 we obtain the two numbers
  64  and  100.

In summary, the polynomial f(x) factors over ℤ (and hence over ℚ) exactly when
  n ∈ {15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100}.

Now, why does “factors over ℚ” imply that f is splitty? (And conversely, if f is irreducible over ℚ then by a theorem of Chebotarev there are infinitely many primes p for which f remains irreducible mod p – in fact, f mod p would then be an irreducible quartic, and no factorization into two polynomials of degree < 4 exists.) In our situation the factorization over ℤ shows that for every prime p the factorization “lifts” modulo p (with the possible exception of finitely many primes dividing some coefficients – but then the factorization still breaks f mod p as a product of two polynomials of degree at most 2).

Thus f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty if and only if n is one of
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100.

Since we are to sum all positive integers n ≤ 100 having the property, we add these numbers:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

Therefore, the answer is 472.

────────────────────────────
Outline of the reasoning:

1. The “splitty‐property” means that for every prime p the polynomial f(x) factors modulo p as a product of two polynomials of degree less than 4. (Since f has degree 4 the only possibilities are a (1,3) split or a (2,2) split.)

2. One may show that if f is irreducible over ℚ then for many primes f remains irreducible modulo p. Hence f is splitty only if it is reducible over ℚ.

3. Writing
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
and comparing coefficients forces A + C = 0 and A(D – B) = 0. In the case A = 0 one obtains (x² + B)(x² + D) with B + D = 16 and BD = n; in the case D = B one obtains (x² + A x + B)(x² – A x + B) with 2B – A² = 16 and B² = n.

4. Solving these equations for positive integers n ≤ 100 produces exactly the nine numbers listed above.

5. Their sum is 472.

────────────────────────────
Final Answer: 472.

We will show that the “splitty‐property” for a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] of degree 4

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

(which we call “splitty” if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] of degree < 4 with
  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) ≡ 0 (mod p))
turns out to be equivalent to f having a non‐trivial factorization over ℤ into two quadratic polynomials. (In other words, f must factor as a product of two quadratics with integer coefficients.) Once that is proved, one may then “read off” the possible positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty and add them.

Below we explain this in detail.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the “Splitty” Condition

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4
such that all coefficients of f – gₚ·hₚ are divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p we have

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)  (mod p).

Since f has degree 4 and both gₚ and hₚ have degree < 4, the only possibilities (apart from the “trivial” factorization by a constant, which is not allowed because then one factor would have degree 4) are that the degrees of gₚ and hₚ are 1 and 3 or both 2. In either case f factors nontrivially modulo p.

Conversely, if for every prime p the reduction f mod p factors as a product of two nonconstant polynomials (of degrees adding to 4) then one may take those factors (lifted to ℤ[x]) as gₚ and hₚ. (Note that if f factors over ℤ then for every prime p the same factorization, reduced modulo p, gives a valid factorization.) 

A standard fact (which follows, for example, from the Chebotarev density theorem) is that if a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is irreducible over ℚ then there are infinitely many primes p for which f mod p remains irreducible. Thus the “splitty” condition forces f to factor nontrivially over ℤ.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. When Does f Factor Over ℤ?

Write
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.
Any factorization of f into quadratics must have the form

  f(x) = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D),
with A, B, C, D ∈ ℤ. Expanding the product we get

  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + BD.
Comparing with f(x) = x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n, we obtain the system:
  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + (B + D) = 16,
  (3) AD + BC = 0,
  (4) B·D = n.

Since (1) tells us C = –A, equation (3) becomes
  A·D + B·(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either A = 0 or D = B.

• Case 1. A = 0.
Then C = 0 and (2) becomes
  0 + (B + D) = 16 ⟹ B + D = 16,
while (4) tells us n = B·D.
In other words, if we can write 16 as a sum of two positive integers B and D whose product is n, then
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D).
In this case f factors over ℤ and, consequently, for every prime p
  f(x) ≡ (x² + B)(x² + D) (mod p).
Thus f is splitty.

Now, B and D are positive integers with B + D = 16. Writing B = b and D = 16 – b (with 1 ≤ b ≤ 15 so that both are positive) we have
  n = b(16 – b).
For b = 1, 2, …, 15 this produces the values
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 63, 60, 55, 48, 39, 28, 15.
The distinct positive values are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.

• Case 2. A ≠ 0 so that D = B.
Then (2) becomes
  A(–A) + 2B = 16 ⟹ –A² + 2B = 16 ⟹ 2B = 16 + A²,
so that
  B = (16 + A²)/2.
Also, (4) gives n = B² = ((16 + A²)/2)².
For n to be an integer we must have 16 + A² even. (Note that if A is odd then A² is odd and 16 + A² is odd; hence A must be even.) Write A = 2k. Then
  B = (16 + 4k²)/2 = 8 + 2k²  and  n = (8 + 2k²)².
For n ≤ 100 we check small k:
  k = 0: n = 8² = 64.
  k = ±1: n = (8 + 2)² = 10² = 100.
  k = ±2: n = (8 + 8)² = 16² = 256, which is too big.
Thus from Case 2 we obtain n = 64 (again) and n = 100.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Conclusion and Summing the n Values

We have shown that f(x) is splitty if and only if it factors over ℤ as a product of two quadratics. In our situation the only possibilities (with n > 0 and n ≤ 100) are those coming from Case 1 and Case 2. In summary, the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
is splitty are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, and 100.

Finally, we compute the sum:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 such that x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 472.

We will show that a polynomial

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n   (with n a positive integer)

has the “splitty” property (namely, that for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) having all coefficients divisible by p) if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℤ. (In other words, f is “splitty” exactly when it is reducible in ℤ[x].) In what follows we explain this and then determine exactly for which n ≤ 100 the polynomial is splitty.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Why “splitty” ⇔ “reducible over ℤ”

Suppose that for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with
  deg(gₚ), deg(hₚ) < deg(f) = 4
such that
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

In particular, for each prime p the reduction f(x) mod p factors as a product of two nonconstant polynomials (of degrees adding to 4). (Note that if one factor were constant then the other would have degree 4, which is not allowed.) One may show (using, for example, a “density‐theoretic” argument or a well‐known fact from algebra) that if a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible over ℚ then there are infinitely many primes p for which its reduction mod p remains irreducible. (For example, x⁴ + 1 is irreducible over ℤ and remains irreducible mod p for infinitely many p.) Thus if f were irreducible over ℤ then there would be some prime p for which no factorization into two polynomials of degree less than 4 exists modulo p. In other words, f is splitty if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℤ.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Factorizing f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n over ℤ

Any factorization of f(x) into two nonconstant polynomials in ℤ[x] must have both factors of degree at most 3. (A factorization into a linear and a cubic would force an integer root r satisfying r⁴ + 16r² + n = 0; but for any nonzero integer r the left‐side is positive, and for r = 0 we get n = 0. Thus the only possibility is a factorization into two quadratics.)

So suppose
  f(x) = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
with A, B, C, D ∈ ℤ. Multiplying out we get
  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + B C)x + B D.
Comparing with
  x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n,

  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + B C = 0,
  (4) B D = n.

Since (1) tells us C = –A, substitute into (2) and (3). Then
  (2) becomes –A² + B + D = 16            [since AC = –A²],
  (3) becomes A·D + B·(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

• Case 1. A = 0, or
• Case 2. D = B.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. A = 0

Then C = 0 and (2) becomes
  B + D = 16,
while (4) is
  B·D = n.

  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + (16 – B)),

We will show that the “splitty‐polynomial” condition

  “For every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg(gₚ),deg(hₚ) < deg(f) such that all the coefficients of f – gₚ hₚ are divisible by p”

is equivalent to the statement that f factors nontrivially over ℚ. (In other words, f is splitty if and only if f is reducible in ℚ[x].) In our problem f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n and we wish to find all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty.

Below is one way to arrive at the answer.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Why “splitty” ⇔ “reducible over ℚ”

Suppose first that f factors nontrivially over ℚ. (That is, f = g h with g,h in ℚ[x] and 0 < deg(g),deg(h) < deg(f).) Clearing denominators we may assume g,h have integer coefficients. Then for any prime p not dividing the “content” (which is 1 in our case) the reduction mod p gives a factorization
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x) hₚ(x) (mod p)
with deg(gₚ),deg(hₚ) < 4. (For the few “exceptional” primes dividing some coefficients the factorization can be checked separately.) Hence f is splitty.

Conversely, if f is splitty then for every prime p the reduction f(x) mod p factors nontrivially. A standard fact (which can be deduced from the Chebotarev density theorem or from properties of irreducible polynomials) is that if f is irreducible over ℚ then f(x) mod p is irreducible for infinitely many primes p. Thus f must be reducible over ℚ.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. Factorizing f(x)= x⁴ + 16x² + n over ℚ

Since f is a quartic with no x³– or x–term it is natural to try a factorization into quadratics. Write

  f(x) = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D).

Expanding we get
  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + B C)x + B D.
Matching with f(x)= x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n we obtain:
  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + B C = 0,
  (4) B D = n.

It is convenient to set C = –A. Then (2) becomes
  –A² + B + D = 16  ⟹ B + D = 16 + A²,
and (3) becomes
  A(D – B) = 0.
Thus we have two cases.

Case I. A = 0.
Then C = 0 and (2) tells us B + D = 16 while (4) gives B·D = n. In other words, f factors as
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D)
with B + D = 16 and B·D = n. (Since the factors have no x–term the degrees are 2, which is less than 4.) For integer B the possible values of n are
  n = B(16 – B).
As B runs through 1, 2, …, 15 (we need n > 0) the distinct values obtained are
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
(Notice that B = 8 gives n = 8·8 = 64 and the symmetry B ↔ 16–B shows the list is symmetric.)

Case II. D = B.
Then (2) becomes
  –A² + 2B = 16  ⟹ 2B = 16 + A² ⟹ B = 8 + (A²)/2.
For B to be an integer we must have A even. Write A = 2k. Then B = 8 + 2k² and (4) becomes
  n = B² = (8 + 2k²)².
For n ≤ 100 the only possibilities are:
  • k = 0 ⟹ n = 8² = 64,
  • k = ±1 ⟹ n = (8 + 2)² = 10² = 100.

We will show that the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

has the “splitty” property (that is, for every prime p one may “almost factor” f over ℤ[x] modulo p into two nonconstant polynomials of degree less than 4) if and only if

  64 – n is a perfect square in ℤ.

In particular, when n is a positive integer not exceeding 100 the “splitty‐condition” forces

  n = 64 – k²  with k² < 64  (i.e. |k| ≤ 7).

A short calculation shows that the possible values are

  n = 64, 63, 60, 55, 48, 39, 28, 15.

Their sum is 64 + 63 + 60 + 55 + 48 + 39 + 28 + 15 = 372.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A little background

We say that a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is “splitty” if for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] of degree less than deg f such that every coefficient of f – gₚ hₚ is divisible by p. (In other words, modulo p we have
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) in ℤ/p[x].)
Since deg f = 4 the only non‐trivial factorizations modulo p are as a product of a linear and a cubic or as a product of two quadratics. In either case f is reducible modulo p. (Note that a constant factor is not allowed because then the other factor would have degree 4.) Thus “splitty” is equivalent to the statement that for every prime p the polynomial f is reducible modulo p.

──────────────────────────────
The key idea

Write
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.
A useful rewriting is to complete the square in x²:
  f(x) = (x² + 8)² + (n – 64).
Now, suppose that for some prime p the polynomial f factors nontrivially modulo p. (It might factor as a linear times a cubic or as two quadratics.) In any such factorization one may show that one of the factors “comes from” the quadratic (x² + 8) so that one ends up with an identity of the form
  (x² + 8)² – r² ≡ x⁴ + 16x² + n (mod p)
for some r ∈ ℤ/p. But then
  (x² + 8)² – r² = (x² + 8 – r)(x² + 8 + r)
equals x⁴ + 16x² + (64 – r²). Hence we must have
  64 – r² = n (mod p).
In particular, if f is reducible modulo every prime p then for every odd prime p the number 64 – n must be a square in ℤ/p. (A little thought shows that even in the case when f factors as a product of two quadratics the same conclusion holds.) But by quadratic‐reciprocity an integer m is a square modulo every odd prime if and only if m is a square in ℤ. (Also, when p = 2 one may check separately that f is always reducible modulo 2.) Therefore the “splitty” property for f forces

  64 – n to be a perfect square in ℤ.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion and answer

Thus f is splitty if and only if there is an integer k with

  64 – n = k²  or  n = 64 – k².
Since n > 0 and n ≤ 100 we must have k² < 64 so that |k| ≤ 7. (Also note that when k = 0 we get n = 64.) The possible values are:

  For k = 0: n = 64  
  For k = ±1: n = 63  
  For k = ±2: n = 60  
  For k = ±3: n = 55  
  For k = ±4: n = 48  
  For k = ±5: n = 39  
  For k = ±6: n = 28  
  For k = ±7: n = 15

Their sum is 64 + 63 + 60 + 55 + 48 + 39 + 28 + 15 = 372.

──────────────────────────────
Final answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

We will show that the polynomial

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

is “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 so that every coefficient of f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) is divisible by p) if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℚ. (In other words, f is splitty exactly when it is reducible in ℚ[x].)

Why is this so? One may show that if f is irreducible over ℚ then by a standard result (a “Capelli‐lemma” type fact) there is some prime p for which f remains irreducible modulo p. On the other hand, if f factors nontrivially over ℚ then writing
  f(x) = g(x)·h(x)   (with g,h in ℤ[x] and deg g,deg h < 4)
one may “clear the denominators” (or use the fact that f is monic and its factors can be taken to be primitive) so that for every prime p one may find polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] (which may be obtained by reducing the coefficients modulo p or by a little adjustment) with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

Thus our task reduces to finding all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which
  x⁴ + 16x² + n
factors nontrivially over ℚ.

Because f(x) is an even polynomial (only even powers of x appear) it is natural to try a factorization into quadratics. In fact, one may show that any factorization of f(x) over ℚ must have the form

  (x² + A x + B)(x² – A x + D)         (1)

with A, B, D ∈ ℤ. (To see this, note that if f(x) factors as a product of two quadratics then writing
  (x² + Cx + E)(x² + Fx + G)
and comparing with f(x) forces C + F = 0 so that F = –C; then writing A = C and renaming E, G as B and D yields (1).)

Multiplying out (1) we get
  (x² + A x + B)(x² – A x + D) = x⁴ + (B + D – A²)x² + (A(D – B))x + B·D.
Since f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n has no x³‐ or x‐term, we must have

  A + (–A) = 0      (automatically true)
  A(D – B) = 0       (so either A = 0 or D = B)
  B + D – A² = 16
  B·D = n.

There are two cases.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. A = 0.

Then (1) becomes
  (x² + B)(x² + D) = x⁴ + (B + D)x² + B·D.
Comparing with f(x) we must have
  B + D = 16  and  B·D = n.
Thus, for any factorization of f(x) in this case the number n is given by
  n = B(16 – B)
with B an integer. (Note that since n > 0 we must have B > 0 and also 16 – B > 0, so 1 ≤ B ≤ 15.) A short computation shows:

  B = 1 → n = 1·15 = 15  
  B = 2 → n = 2·14 = 28  
  B = 3 → n = 3·13 = 39  
  B = 4 → n = 4·12 = 48  
  B = 5 → n = 5·11 = 55  
  B = 6 → n = 6·10 = 60  
  B = 7 → n = 7·9  = 63  
  B = 8 → n = 8·8  = 64  
  B = 9 → n = 9·7  = 63  (repeat)  
  B = 10 → n = 10·6 = 60  (repeat)  
  … and so on.

Thus the distinct values of n coming from Case 1 (with 1 ≤ B ≤ 15) are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
──────────────────────────────
Case 2. D = B.

Then (1) becomes
  (x² + A x + B)(x² – A x + B) = x⁴ + (2B – A²)x² + B².
Comparing with f(x) we must have
  2B – A² = 16  and  B² = n.
That is, n must be a perfect square (n = B²) and
  A² = 2B – 16.
For A to be an integer we need 2B – 16 to be a perfect square. Write A = 2k (since if A were odd then 2B – 16 would be odd, impossible because 2B is even). Then
  (2k)² = 4k² = 2B – 16  ⟹  B = 2k² + 8.
Also, n = B² = (2k² + 8)².
We now require n ≤ 100.
• For k = 0: B = 8, n = 64.
• For k = 1: B = 2 + 8 = 10, n = 100.
• For k = 2: B = 8 + 8 = 16, n = 256 (too big).
Thus the only new value from Case 2 is n = 100 (note that n = 64 already appeared in Case 1).

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The polynomial f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n factors over ℚ (and hence is splitty) exactly when

  n ∈ {15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100}.

We are asked to compute the sum of all such positive integers n ≤ 100. Adding these values we get:

  15 + 28 = 43  
  43 + 39 = 82  
  82 + 48 = 130  
  130 + 55 = 185  
  185 + 60 = 245  
  245 + 63 = 308  
  308 + 64 = 372  
  372 + 100 = 472.

Thus, the desired sum is 472.

We wish to decide for which positive integers n ≤ 100 the polynomial

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

is “splitty.” By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with

  deg(gₚ) < deg(f) and deg(hₚ) < deg(f)

such that every coefficient of f – gₚ·hₚ is divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p the congruence

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p)

holds (as polynomials), with both gₚ and hₚ having degree less than 4.

An equivalent way to state this is that for every prime p the polynomial f factors nontrivially modulo p (i.e. it is reducible in ℤ/pℤ[x]). (Note that if f were irreducible modulo some prime p, then no such factorization with factors of degree less than 4 could exist.)

Step 1. Rewrite f(x) in a suggestive form.

Notice that
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = x⁴ + 16x² + 64 + (n – 64)
           = (x² + 8)² + (n – 64).

It is even more convenient to write this as
  f(x) = (x² + 8)² – (64 – n).

Step 2. Factorization Modulo p

For any prime p, if we can “take square roots” modulo p then we can factor f(x) as follows. Suppose that in ℤ/pℤ the number 64 – n is a square. That is, there exists some a in ℤ/pℤ with

  a² = 64 – n  (mod p).

Then we may write
  (x² + 8)² – a² = (x² + 8 – a)(x² + 8 + a).

Since the factors x² + 8 – a and x² + 8 + a are quadratic (degree 2) polynomials with coefficients in ℤ/pℤ, we have exhibited a factorization of f(x) modulo p with both factors of degree less than 4.

Conversely, if f(x) factors modulo p nontrivially (with factors of degree less than 4), one may show that necessarily 64 – n is a square modulo p. (For example, if f(x) had a linear factor modulo p, then some r ∈ ℤ/pℤ would satisfy f(r) = 0. But then
  r⁴ + 16r² + n = (r² + 8)² + (n – 64) = 0,
so (r² + 8)² = 64 – n, showing that 64 – n is a square modulo p.)

Thus, the condition that f is splitty (i.e. f factors modulo every prime p) is equivalent to the statement that for every prime p the number 64 – n is a square in ℤ/pℤ.

Step 3. A Global Condition

A classical fact from number theory (the local–global principle for quadratic forms) tells us that an integer d is a square in every ℤ/pℤ (for all primes p) if and only if d is a square in ℚ – and for integers this means that d must be a perfect square (possibly 0).

Thus, for f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n to be splitty we must have

  64 – n = m²  for some m ∈ ℤ.

Since n is a positive integer and we are only considering n ≤ 100, note that if 64 – n were negative then it could not be a (nonnegative) perfect square. Therefore we must have

  64 – n ≥ 0 ⟹ n ≤ 64.

Step 4. Find the admissible n

Write
  64 – n = m²  ⟹  n = 64 – m²,
where m is a nonnegative integer. Also, since n > 0 we require m² < 64 so that m can be 0, 1, 2, …, 7. This gives:

  m = 0 ⟹ n = 64 – 0 = 64  
  m = 1 ⟹ n = 64 – 1 = 63  
  m = 2 ⟹ n = 64 – 4 = 60  
  m = 3 ⟹ n = 64 – 9 = 55  
  m = 4 ⟹ n = 64 – 16 = 48  
  m = 5 ⟹ n = 64 – 25 = 39  
  m = 6 ⟹ n = 64 – 36 = 28  
  m = 7 ⟹ n = 64 – 49 = 15

Thus the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty are:

  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.

Step 5. Compute the Sum

Now, we add these values:

  15 + 28 = 43  
  43 + 39 = 82  
  82 + 48 = 130  
  130 + 55 = 185  
  185 + 60 = 245  
  245 + 63 = 308  
  308 + 64 = 372

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

Final Answer: 372.

We will show that the polynomial

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

is “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) mod p) if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℤ. (In our situation “nontrivial” means that neither factor is a constant polynomial.) Once we know this, the problem reduces to finding all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f factors over ℤ as a product of two polynomials of degree less than 4.

Step 1. Why “splitty” ⇔ reducible over ℤ

A polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is called splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < deg f
and
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).

Notice that if f factors nontrivially over ℤ as
  f(x) = g(x)·h(x)
with 0 < deg g, deg h < deg f, then for every prime p the reduction modulo p gives
  f(x) ≡ g(x)·h(x) (mod p),
so the condition is satisfied.

Conversely, if f is splitty then for every prime p the polynomial f mod p factors as a product of two nonconstant polynomials. A standard fact (which follows, for example, from the Chebotarev density theorem or from results on irreducibility modulo primes) is that if f is irreducible over ℚ then there are infinitely many primes p for which f mod p remains irreducible. Hence f must be reducible over ℚ and, since f ∈ ℤ[x] is primitive, it factors nontrivially over ℤ.

Thus, f is splitty if and only if it factors nontrivially in ℤ[x] with factors of degree less than 4.

Step 2. What factorizations are possible for f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n?

Since f is a quartic (degree 4) and is monic, any nonconstant factorization must be as a product of two quadratics. (A factorization into a linear and a cubic would force an integer root; but for positive n the equation x⁴ + 16x² + n = 0 has no integer solution.)

So we look for a factorization of the form

  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + Ax + B)(x² + Cx + D)
with A, B, C, D ∈ ℤ.

Expanding the product we get

  (x² + Ax + B)(x² + Cx + D) = x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + BD.

Matching coefficients with x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n we obtain the system:
  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + BC = 0,
  (4) B·D = n.

There are two cases to consider.

Case I. A = 0.

Then C = 0 and the equations become:
  B + D = 16    (from (2))
  B·D = n     (from (4)).

Thus, if we can find integers B and D with B + D = 16 and B·D = n, then
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + B)(x² + D).

For positive n we must have B and D positive. Writing B and D as the two numbers whose sum is 16 and product is n, we see that the possible pairs (B, D) (up to order) are:
  (1, 15) → n = 15,
  (2, 14) → n = 28,
  (3, 13) → n = 39,
  (4, 12) → n = 48,
  (5, 11) → n = 55,
  (6, 10) → n = 60,
  (7, 9)  → n = 63,
  (8, 8)  → n = 64.

Case II. D = B.

Then equation (3) is automatically satisfied. With D = B, equation (2) becomes:
  AC + 2B = 16.
But from (1) we have C = –A so that AC = –A². Hence
  –A² + 2B = 16  ⟹ 2B = 16 + A² ⟹ B = (16 + A²)/2.
Since B must be an integer, A² must be even; that is, A must be even. Write A = 2k with k ∈ ℤ. Then
  B = (16 + 4k²)/2 = 8 + 2k².
Also, equation (4) becomes
  B² = n.
We need n ≤ 100. For k = 0 we get B = 8 and n = 64 (which we already obtained). For k = ±1 we get B = 8 + 2 = 10 and n = 10² = 100. For |k| ≥ 2 the value of n exceeds 100. Thus, from this case we obtain n = 100.

Step 3. List all n ≤ 100 for which f factors over ℤ

From Case I we obtained:
  n = 15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
From Case II we obtained:
  n = 100.

Thus, the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, and 100.

Step 4. Compute the sum

Add these values:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 472.

Final Answer: 472.

We wish to decide for which positive integers n ≤ 100 the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

has the following property (“splitty”): For every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with

  deg(gₚ) < deg(f) and deg(hₚ) < deg(f)

such that all coefficients of f – gₚ·hₚ are divisible by p.

Because deg(f) = 4, the condition means that for every prime p the polynomial f(x) (when reduced modulo p) factors as a product of two polynomials of degree less than 4. (Note that a “factorization” into a constant times a degree‑3 polynomial is not allowed since the constant factor would have degree 0 and the other factor degree 3; but then the product would have degree 3, not 4. In fact, since the leading coefficient of f is 1 (which is never 0 mod p), the only possibilities are a factorization into a linear and a cubic factor or into two quadratics.)

A key observation is that if f factors over ℤ as a product of two quadratics, then for every prime p the reduction modulo p gives a valid factorization into two quadratics (since the leading coefficients 1 are never 0 mod p). Conversely, if f is irreducible over ℤ then by a standard theorem (for example, by using properties of Galois groups or by Capelli’s lemma) there will be infinitely many primes p for which f remains irreducible modulo p. Thus f must factor over ℤ into two quadratics.

So we look for a factorization

  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + Ax + B)(x² + Cx + D)

with A, B, C, D ∈ ℤ. Expanding the right‐hand side we get

  (x² + Ax + B)(x² + Cx + D) = x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + BD.

Matching coefficients with f(x) we must have:
1. Coefficient of x³: A + C = 0.
2. Coefficient of x²: AC + (B + D) = 16.
3. Coefficient of x:  AD + BC = 0.
4. Constant term:   BD = n.

Since A + C = 0 we may write C = –A. Then the x-term condition becomes
  AD + B(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either A = 0 or D = B.

• Case 1. If A = 0 then C = 0. The x²–coefficient condition becomes
  (0) + (B + D) = 16 ⟹ B + D = 16.
Also, the constant term is BD = n. In this case f factors as
  (x² + B)(x² + D) with B + D = 16 and BD = n.

• Case 2. If D = B then the x²–coefficient condition becomes

Thus the only possibility in Case 2 that gives no x³–term is k = 0, which reduces to Case 1.

Thus the only possibility is that f factors as
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D)
with B + D = 16 and BD = n.

We will show that for the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

to be “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ in ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with f – gₚhₚ having all coefficients divisible by p), it is necessary and sufficient that the “shifted‐constant”
  64 – n
is a perfect square in ℤ.

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion and then use it to find all n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating “Splitty”

By definition f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4
such that every coefficient of
  f(x) – gₚ(x)hₚ(x)
is divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p we have
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)hₚ(x) (mod p)
with deg(gₚ), deg(hₚ) < 4.

Since f has degree 4 the only way to “split” f modulo p is to write it as a product of two polynomials whose degrees add to 4. (For example, one might have a linear factor times a cubic, or two quadratics.) In particular, f (mod p) must be reducible in Fₚ[x].

Thus, f is splitty if and only if for every prime p the polynomial f(x) is reducible in Fₚ[x].

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A Change of Variable

Notice that f is an even polynomial. Writing
  y = x²
we have
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n = y² + 16y + n.
It is often easier to study a quadratic than a quartic. (Of course, one must be a little careful since a factorization of a quadratic in y need not immediately give a factorization of f in x—but as we will see, it is enough for our purposes.)

Complete the square in y:
  y² + 16y + n = (y + 8)² + (n – 64).
Returning to x (with y = x²) we may write
  f(x) = (x² + 8)² + (n – 64).

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. When Is f(x) Reducible Modulo p?

For an odd prime p (the case p = 2 can be checked separately), one standard way to “force” a factorization is to have the quadratic in y factor. That is, if the quadratic
  Q(y) = y² + 16y + n
factors in Fₚ[y] then its discriminant must be a square in Fₚ. Its discriminant is
  Δ = 16² – 4·1·n = 256 – 4n = 4(64 – n).
Since 4 is a square (2²) in any field of characteristic ≠ 2, we see that Q(y) factors in Fₚ[y] if and only if
  64 – n
is a square in Fₚ.

Now, by a well‐known local–global principle for squares (or by the Chebotarev density theorem) a fixed nonzero integer m is a square modulo every prime p (except those dividing m) if and only if m is a square in ℤ. (Indeed, if m were not a square in ℤ then roughly half the primes would have m nonsquare modulo p.) In our situation m = 64 – n. Thus, for every prime p (with the obvious check at p = 2) the polynomial f(x) factors modulo p if and only if 64 – n is a perfect square in ℤ.

A short check shows that when p = 2 the polynomial
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
reduces modulo 2 to
  x⁴ + n     (since 16 ≡ 0 mod 2),
which is clearly reducible (for if n is odd, x = 1 is a root; if n is even, x⁴ factors as x⁴).

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Conclusion and Finding the n’s

We have shown that f is splitty if and only if for every prime p the polynomial f(x) factors modulo p. And as explained, this happens if and only if the constant 64 – n is a perfect square in ℤ.

Thus, writing
  64 – n = k²    (with k ∈ ℤ)
we deduce that
  n = 64 – k².
Since we want positive integers n ≤ 100 and 64 – n must be nonnegative (because a square in ℤ is nonnegative), we require
  64 – n ≥ 0  ⟹  n ≤ 64.
Also, n > 0. So k² can be 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, or 49. (Note that k = 8 would give 64 – 64 = 0, but then n = 0, which is not positive.) The corresponding values of n are:

  If k = 0: n = 64 – 0 = 64.
  If k = 1: n = 64 – 1 = 63.
  If k = 2: n = 64 – 4 = 60.
  If k = 3: n = 64 – 9 = 55.
  If k = 4: n = 64 – 16 = 48.
  If k = 5: n = 64 – 25 = 39.
  If k = 6: n = 64 – 36 = 28.
  If k = 7: n = 64 – 49 = 15.

These eight numbers (15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64) are exactly the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f(x) is splitty.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Compute the Sum

We now add these values:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

We will show that a monic quartic f(x) ∈ ℤ[x] is “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p))

if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℤ. (In fact, one may prove using Capelli’s lemma that if f is irreducible over ℚ then for infinitely many primes p the reduction f mod p is irreducible.) In our problem the polynomial is

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.

Thus f is splitty exactly when f factors in ℤ[x] as a product of two polynomials of degree less than 4. (Since f is degree 4 the only possibilities are a product of two quadratics or a linear times a cubic. As one may check, a linear–cubic factorization cannot occur in this situation.)

Step 1. Factorization as two quadratics

Suppose
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
with A,B,C,D ∈ ℤ. Expanding the product we get
  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + B C)x + B D.
Comparing with x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n we obtain the system
  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) A·D + B·C = 0,
  (4) B·D = n.
Since (1) tells us C = –A, equation (3) becomes
  A·D – A·B = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

Case 1. A = 0, or

Case 2. D = B.

Let’s analyze each case.

Case 1. A = 0.
Then C = 0 and (2) becomes
  B + D = 16,
while (4) is
  B·D = n.
In other words, if we set B to be any integer and take D = 16 – B, then
  n = B(16 – B).
For n > 0 (and n ≤ 100) we must have B and 16 – B positive. (For example, if B = 1 then D = 15 and n = 15; if B = 2 then n = 28; …; if B = 8 then n = 64; if B = 9 then n = 63; and so on.) In fact, taking B = 1,2,…,15 we obtain the numbers
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
(Notice that B = 9 gives the same value as B = 7, etc., so the distinct positive n in this family are as above.)

Case 2. D = B.
Then (2) becomes
  AC + 2B = 16.
But since C = –A, we have AC = –A² so that
  –A² + 2B = 16 ⟹ 2B = 16 + A² ⟹ B = 8 + ½A².
For B to be an integer we must have A² even, so A is even. Write A = 2k (with k ∈ ℤ). Then
  B = 8 + 2k²,
and (4) gives
  n = B² = (8 + 2k²)².
For n ≤ 100 the only possibilities are:
  • k = 0, which gives n = 8² = 64 (already obtained in Case 1),
  • k = ±1, which gives n = (8 + 2)² = 10² = 100.
For |k| ≥ 2 the value of n is too large.

Thus, the complete list of positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f(x) factors in ℤ[x] (and hence is splitty) is
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100.

Step 2. Summing the values

We now add these numbers:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

Therefore, the sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 472.

Answer: 472.

We will show that the quartic
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
has the “splitty” property (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and
  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)
has all its coefficients divisible by p)
if and only if the constant n is of the form

  n = 64 – k²     (with k an integer, 0 ≤ k² < 64).

In particular, when 0 ≤ k ≤ 7 the possible n (with n > 0 and n ≤ 100) are
  n = 64, 63, 60, 55, 48, 39, 28, 15.
Their sum is 372.

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating “Splitty”

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 such that
  f(x) – gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)
has all coefficients divisible by p. In other words, reducing modulo p we have

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x)  (in ℤ/pℤ[x]).

Since f has degree 4 and the degrees of gₚ and hₚ are both less than 4, the only possible degree‐combinations (in ℤ/pℤ[x]) are
  (1, 3), (2, 2), or (3, 1).
In particular, f(x) must factor (mod p) as a product of two nonconstant polynomials. (Note that a factorization as a constant times a quartic is not allowed because the constant factor would have degree 0, and 0 is not less than 4.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. The Special Form of f(x)

Notice that
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
is an even polynomial (only even powers of x appear). In any factorization modulo an odd prime p (with p not dividing the content of f) the only possible linear factor would have to be x (since if r is a root then –r is also a root, forcing r = –r, i.e. r = 0). Thus, for any odd prime p not dividing n the factorization must be as a product of two quadratics. (For primes p dividing n the situation is easier, as we now explain.)

So assume p is an odd prime with p ∤ n. Then we can write
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + ax + b)(x² + cx + d)
with a, b, c, d in ℤ/pℤ. Expanding and equating coefficients we obtain:
  a + c = 0               [coefficient of x³]
  ac + (b + d) = 16        [coefficient of x²]
  ad + bc = 0            [coefficient of x]
  bd = n               [constant term]

A natural choice is to take a = 0 (which forces c = 0). Then the equations become:
  b + d = 16  and bd = n.
That is, we must be able to write n as the product of two numbers b and d in ℤ/pℤ that add up to 16. But thinking of t as an indeterminate, the pair (b, d) is determined by the quadratic
  t² – 16t + n = 0.
Its discriminant is
  Δ = 16² – 4n = 256 – 4n = 4(64 – n).
For an odd prime p not dividing n the constant 4 is a square (since 2² = 4 in ℤ/pℤ), so the condition that Δ be a square in ℤ/pℤ is equivalent to requiring that 64 – n be a square in ℤ/pℤ.

Thus, for every odd prime p not dividing n we must have that 64 – n is a quadratic residue modulo p. But it is a standard fact from number theory that if m is a nonzero integer which is not a perfect square in ℤ, then there are infinitely many primes for which m is not a square modulo p. (In fact, the set of primes for which a fixed nonzero integer is a quadratic residue has asymptotic density ½.) Hence the only way that 64 – n can be a square modulo every odd prime (other than those dividing n) is that 64 – n is a perfect square as an integer. (In the case when 64 – n = 0, i.e. n = 64, the condition is automatically met for all p since then f(x) factors as (x²+8)².)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. The p = 2 Case

When p = 2, note that 16 ≡ 0 (mod 2) so
  f(x) ≡ x⁴ + n  (mod 2).
There are two cases:
• If n is even then f(x) ≡ x⁴, which factors as x·x³ (or even as x²·x²), so the condition is met.
• If n is odd then f(x) ≡ x⁴ + 1. But in ℤ/2ℤ one may check that
  x⁴ + 1 = (x² + 1)²,
since (x² + 1)² = x⁴ + 2x² + 1 and 2x² ≡ 0 (mod 2). Thus the factorization exists.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Conclusion and Finding n ≤ 100

We have shown that f(x) is splitty if and only if for every odd prime p not dividing n the number 64 – n is a square modulo p. This forces 64 – n to be a perfect square as an integer. Write
  64 – n = k²             (with k an integer).
Then
  n = 64 – k².
Since n must be positive and at most 100, we require
  0 < 64 – k² ≤ 100.
The inequality 64 – k² > 0 gives k² < 64, so k can be 0, 1, 2, …, 7. (The case k = 0 gives n = 64.) Thus the possible values of n are:
  for k = 0: n = 64;
  for k = 1: n = 64 – 1 = 63;
  for k = 2: n = 64 – 4 = 60;
  for k = 3: n = 64 – 9 = 55;
  for k = 4: n = 64 – 16 = 48;
  for k = 5: n = 64 – 25 = 39;
  for k = 6: n = 64 – 36 = 28;
  for k = 7: n = 64 – 49 = 15.
These are all ≤ 100.

Finally, we compute their sum:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

Then we are asked: "Compute the sum of all positive integers n <= 100 such that the polynomial x^4 + 16x^2 + n is splitty."
