We will show that the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

has the “splitty” property (namely, that for every prime p there exist nonconstant polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and f(x) – gₚ(x)hₚ(x) having all coefficients divisible by p) if and only if n is a positive integer at most 64 for which

  64 – n

is a perfect square. In that case one may even exhibit an explicit factorization over ℤₚ.

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating “Splitty”

By definition f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with
  deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4
such that every coefficient of
  f(x) – gₚ(x)hₚ(x)
is divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p the polynomial f(x) is congruent modulo p to a product of two nonconstant polynomials (since a constant factor is allowed but then the other factor would have degree 4, which is not allowed). In particular, f must be reducible modulo p in a non‐trivial way.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A Change of View

Notice that
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n
may be “completed” in the variable x². Writing y = x² we have
  f(x) = y² + 16y + n.
In any field (or ℤₚ) a quadratic factors nontrivially if and only if its discriminant is a square. Here the discriminant is
  Δ = 16² – 4·1·n = 256 – 4n = 4(64 – n).
Thus, over any field in which 4 is a square (which is automatic in ℤₚ for any odd p, and trivial for p = 2) the quadratic y² + 16y + n factors if and only if 64 – n is a square in that field.

Now, if y² + 16y + n factors as
  (y – r)(y – s)
with r + s = 16 and rs = n, then one may “lift” this factorization to x by writing
  f(x) = (x² – r)(x² – s).
In ℤₚ the factors x² – r and x² – s have degree 2 (unless one of r or s is 0, but then the factor is still nonconstant) and 2 < 4. Hence f is splitty (i.e. f factors nontrivially modulo every prime) provided that for every prime p the number 64 – n is a square in ℤₚ.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. When Is 64 – n a Square Modulo Every Prime?

A basic fact from number theory is that an integer m is a square modulo every prime p if and only if m is a perfect square in ℤ. (For if m were not a perfect square in ℤ then some prime q would appear to an odd power in m and for p = q the number m would be 0 modulo q – which is a square – but for some other prime p not dividing m the Legendre symbol (m/p) would be –1.) 

Thus, for our f(x) the condition that for every prime p the discriminant 4(64 – n) is a square in ℤₚ is equivalent to requiring that 64 – n is a perfect square in ℤ. In other words, there must exist an integer k such that

  64 – n = k²        (1)

or, equivalently,

  n = 64 – k².

Since we are only interested in positive integers n (and n ≤ 100 by the problem’s statement), we must have n > 0 and also 64 – n ≥ 0 (because a perfect square in ℤ is nonnegative). Thus n ≤ 64 and k² ≤ 64.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Determining the Possible Values of n

The nonnegative perfect squares not exceeding 64 are:
  0² = 0, 1² = 1, 2² = 4, 3² = 9, 4² = 16, 5² = 25, 6² = 36, 7² = 49, 8² = 64.
If we set 64 – n = k² then
  n = 64 – k².
We must have n > 0 so k² cannot be 64 (which would give n = 0). Thus the acceptable choices are for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. This yields:
  k = 0: n = 64 – 0 = 64
  k = 1: n = 64 – 1 = 63
  k = 2: n = 64 – 4 = 60
  k = 3: n = 64 – 9 = 55
  k = 4: n = 64 – 16 = 48
  k = 5: n = 64 – 25 = 39
  k = 6: n = 64 – 36 = 28
  k = 7: n = 64 – 49 = 15

These are all ≤ 64 and hence ≤ 100.

For each such n the polynomial factors (over ℤₚ for every prime p) as
  f(x) = (x² + 8 – k)(x² + 8 + k)
since
  (x² + 8 – k)(x² + 8 + k) = x⁴ + 16x² + (64 – k²) = x⁴ + 16x² + n.
Thus f is splitty for exactly these values of n.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Summing the Valid n

We now add the eight valid values:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
A quick calculation gives:
  15 + 28 = 43
  43 + 39 = 82
  82 + 48 = 130
  130 + 55 = 185
  185 + 60 = 245
  245 + 63 = 308
  308 + 64 = 372

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which the polynomial x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

Thus, the final answer is 372.

We will show that the “splitty‐condition”
  “For every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with deg gₚ,deg hₚ < deg f such that all coefficients of f – gₚ·hₚ are divisible by p”
for a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] is equivalent to f being reducible over ℚ. (In our situation f has degree 4, so “deg < 4” means the factors must be of degree at most 3; in fact, as we will see, the only possibility is a factorization into two quadratics.)

Once this is proved, the problem reduces to finding all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

factors nontrivially over ℚ. (Then for every prime p the factorization over ℤ will reduce mod p to give factors of degree less than 4.)

Below is one way to arrive at the answer.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Reformulating “splitty”

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with deg gₚ,deg hₚ < 4 such that
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p).
In other words, for every prime p the polynomial f factors (nontrivially) in ℤ/pℤ. (Note that the “trivial” factorization f = (constant)·f is not allowed since deg f = 4 is not less than 4.) 

A standard fact in number theory is that if a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible over ℚ then it remains irreducible modulo infinitely many primes. (This is sometimes called “Schur’s theorem” or is a consequence of the fact that a polynomial which is irreducible over ℚ cannot have a non‐trivial factorization in every finite field.) Hence, if f is splitty then f must be reducible over ℚ. Conversely, if f factors nontrivially over ℚ then by reducing the factorization modulo p one obtains a factorization in ℤ/pℤ (with factors of degree less than 4). Thus f is splitty if and only if f is reducible over ℚ.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. When is f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n reducible over ℚ?

Because f has no x³‐ or x‐term, it is natural to set
  y = x².
Then
  f(x) = (x²)² + 16·(x²) + n = y² + 16y + n.
Thus f factors over ℚ if and only if the quadratic in y,
  y² + 16y + n,
factors over ℚ. (Once it factors in y, one may “pull back” the factorization to x by writing each factor as x² + (constant).)

A quadratic with integer coefficients factors over ℚ exactly when its discriminant is a perfect square. Here the discriminant is
  Δ = 16² – 4·n = 256 – 4n.
So we need an integer m such that
  256 – 4n = m².
It is convenient to write m = 2k (since 256 is divisible by 4, m must be even). Then
  256 – 4n = 4k² ⟹ 4n = 256 – 4k² ⟹ n = 64 – k².
Thus f factors over ℚ if and only if
  n = 64 – k²  for some integer k.

Since we are interested in positive n ≤ 100, we require
  64 – k² > 0 ⟹ k² < 64 ⟹ |k| ≤ 7.
(The value k = ±8 would give n = 0, which is not positive.)

For k = 0, ±1, ±2, …, ±7 the possible values of n are:
  k = 0: n = 64;
  k = ±1: n = 64 – 1 = 63;
  k = ±2: n = 64 – 4 = 60;
  k = ±3: n = 64 – 9 = 55;
  k = ±4: n = 64 – 16 = 48;
  k = ±5: n = 64 – 25 = 39;
  k = ±6: n = 64 – 36 = 28;
  k = ±7: n = 64 – 49 = 15.
These give the eight distinct positive integers
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
(Notice that for example when k = 1 and k = –1 we get the same n = 63.)

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. Conclusion

We have shown that f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty (i.e. f factors mod every prime p into factors of degree less than 4) if and only if it factors over ℚ. And the factorization over ℚ occurs precisely when
  n = 64 – k² for some integer k with |k| ≤ 7.
Thus the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f is splitty are exactly
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.

The problem asks for the sum of these n. We compute:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372.

───────────────────────────── 
Answer

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 such that x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

We will show that the given quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

is “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < 4 and f(x) – gₚ(x)hₚ(x) having all coefficients divisible by p) if and only if

  64 – n is a perfect square (in ℤ).

In particular, when n is a positive integer with n ≤ 100, f is splitty exactly when

  n = 64 – k²  for some integer k.

Once we have this, we list the possible values and add them.

Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Reformulating “Splitty”

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg(gₚ), deg(hₚ) < 4 such that

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x) hₚ(x) (mod p).

Since f is degree 4 the only non‐trivial factorizations (with both factors nonconstant) are as a product of two quadratics. (A factorization involving a linear factor would force an integer root of f, but one may check that x⁴ + 16x² + n has no integer roots for n ≠ 0.) Thus for every prime p the reduction f(x) mod p factors as

  f(x) ≡ (x² + β)(x² + δ)  (in Fₚ[x]),

for some β, δ in Fₚ. Expanding we get

  (x² + β)(x² + δ) = x⁴ + (β + δ)x² + βδ.

Comparing with f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n we deduce that
  β + δ = 16  and  βδ = n.

In other words, if we think of β and δ as the two roots of the quadratic

  t² – 16t + n = 0,
 
then for every odd prime p the existence of β, δ in Fₚ is equivalent to the discriminant

  Δ = 16² – 4n = 256 – 4n

being a square in Fₚ. (For p = 2 the condition is automatic since 256 – 4n ≡ 0 mod 2.) Notice that for odd primes the factor 4 is a square (since 2² = 4), so for odd p we have

  256 – 4n is a square in Fₚ ⟺ 64 – n is a square in Fₚ.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. For “Every Prime” the Only Possibility

A classical fact from number theory is that if a fixed nonzero integer a is not a perfect square in ℤ then there are infinitely many primes p for which a is a quadratic non‐residue modulo p. (In symbols, (a/p) = –1 for infinitely many p.) Therefore, in order that 64 – n be a square in Fₚ for every odd prime p, it is necessary that 64 – n actually be a perfect square in ℤ. (The case 64 – n = 0 is allowed since 0 is a square.)

Thus we conclude that f is splitty if and only if

  64 – n = k²  for some integer k,
or equivalently,
  n = 64 – k².

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. Finding All n ≤ 100

We now need the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which n = 64 – k² for some integer k.

Since n > 0 we must have 64 – k² > 0, so k² < 64. The nonnegative integers k with k² < 64 are

  k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

For each we compute n:

  k = 0: n = 64 – 0 = 64  
  k = 1: n = 64 – 1 = 63  
  k = 2: n = 64 – 4 = 60  
  k = 3: n = 64 – 9 = 55  
  k = 4: n = 64 – 16 = 48  
  k = 5: n = 64 – 25 = 39  
  k = 6: n = 64 – 36 = 28  
  k = 7: n = 64 – 49 = 15

All these values are positive and clearly ≤ 100.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 4. Summing the Values

We now add the eight values:

  15 + 28 + 39 + 48 + 55 + 60 + 63 + 64.

A quick calculation:

  15 + 28 = 43  
  43 + 39 = 82  
  82 + 48 = 130  
  130 + 55 = 185  
  185 + 60 = 245  
  245 + 63 = 308  
  308 + 64 = 372

───────────────────────────── 
Conclusion

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which the polynomial x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 372.

We will show that the “splitty‐property” for 
  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n 
forces f to factor nontrivially over ℤ (and hence over ℤ/p for every prime p). In other words, one may prove that if f is “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ in ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with 
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p)),
then in fact f must factor over ℤ as a product of two polynomials of degree less than 4. (Conversely, if f factors over ℤ then reducing the factors modulo any prime gives the required representation.) In our situation f is a quartic so the only possibilities are a factorization as a product of two quadratics or as a product of a linear and a cubic. (A linear factor would force f(0)=n = 0, but n is positive.) Thus f must split as

  f(x) = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D)
with A, B, C, D ∈ ℤ.

A short calculation shows that
  (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D) 
expands as
  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + B C)x + B D.
Comparing with
  x⁴ + 0·x³ + 16x² + 0·x + n,
we deduce that
  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + B C = 0,
  (4) B D = n.

There are two cases.

• Case 1. A = 0.
Then C = 0 and (2) becomes B + D = 16 while (4) says B·D = n. In other words, writing B and D as two numbers whose sum is 16 and product is n, we see that
  n = B(16 – B)
for some integer B. (In this case the factorization is
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + (16 – B)).)

• Case 2. D = B.
Then (3) is automatically satisfied and (2) becomes
  AC + 2B = 16.
But since A + C = 0 (so C = –A) we have AC = –A² and hence
  –A² + 2B = 16 ⟹ 2B = 16 + A² ⟹ B = 8 + (A²)/2.
For B to be an integer we must have A even. Write A = 2k; then B = 8 + 2k² and (4) gives
  n = B² = [8 + 2k²]² = 4(4 + k²)².
For n ≤ 100 the only possibilities occur when k = 0 (giving n = 64) or k = ±1 (giving n = 4(4+1)² = 100). (The next value, k = ±2, would yield n = 4(4+4)² = 256 > 100.)

Thus, if f factors over ℤ then necessarily
  n = B(16 – B) for some integer B  or  n = 100.
When B runs through the integers 1, 2, …, 15 (since n must be positive and ≤ 100) the values of B(16 – B) are:
  1·15 = 15,
  2·14 = 28,
  3·13 = 39,
  4·12 = 48,
  5·11 = 55,
  6·10 = 60,
  7·9  = 63,
  8·8  = 64.
(Notice that B = 9, 10, …, 15 give the same numbers as above.) In addition we get n = 100 from Case 2.

A standard theorem (Schur’s theorem) tells us that if a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible over ℚ then there are infinitely many primes p for which it remains irreducible modulo p.   15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, and 100.

We will show that a polynomial f(x) ∈ ℤ[x] has the “splitty” property (namely, that for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] of degree less than deg f with 
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p))
if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℚ (and hence over ℤ after clearing denominators). (In fact, one may prove by “Capelli’s lemma” that if f is irreducible over ℚ then for some prime p the reduction f mod p is irreducible; conversely, if f factors nontrivially over ℚ then one may “lift” that factorization modulo every prime.) 

In our problem the polynomial is

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n      (1)

with n a positive integer (n ≤ 100). Thus f is splitty exactly when f factors nontrivially in ℤ[x] (that is, it is reducible over ℚ).

A standard way to factor a quartic with no x³‐ or x‐term is to try a factorization into two quadratics. So assume
  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + a x + b)(x² + c x + d)
with a, b, c, d ∈ ℤ. Expanding the right‐side we get

  (x² + a x + b)(x² + c x + d)
    = x⁴ + (a + c)x³ + (ac + b + d)x² + (ad + b c)x + b d.

Comparing with (1) we must have

  (1) a + c = 0,
  (2) ac + (b + d) = 16,
  (3) ad + b c = 0,
  (4) b d = n.

Since (1) tells us a + c = 0, write c = –a. Then (2) becomes
  –a² + (b + d) = 16   ⇒ b + d = 16 + a².
Also, (3) becomes
  a d + b(–a) = a(d – b) = 0.
Thus we have two cases:

• Case 1. a = 0.
 Then c = 0 and (2) gives b + d = 16 while (4) gives n = b·d.
 In other words, if we can write
  n = b(16 – b)
for some integer b then f factors as

has the “splitty” property (that is, for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] of degree less than 4 with f(x) – gₚ(x)hₚ(x) having all coefficients divisible by p) if and only if f factors nontrivially over ℤ (in fact, as a product of two quadratics). Once we prove this “if and only if” fact, the problem reduces to finding all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which

  x⁴ + 16x² + n

can be factored as a product of two quadratics with integer coefficients.

Below we explain these two steps.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Why “splitty” ⇔ reducible over ℤ

By definition, f is splitty if for every prime p there exist gₚ,hₚ ∈ ℤ[x] with deg gₚ, deg hₚ < deg f (here deg f = 4) so that
  f(x) – gₚ(x)hₚ(x)
has all its coefficients divisible by p. In other words, for every prime p we have
  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)hₚ(x)  (mod p).
In the finite field Fₚ the factors gₚ and hₚ have degrees less than 4 and their product has degree at most 6. But since f has degree 4 the only possibility is that the factorization “uses up” the degree 4. (A factorization into a constant times a degree‑4 polynomial is not allowed because then one factor would have degree 0.) In particular, f (mod p) factors as a product of two polynomials of degrees 1 and 3 or of two quadratics.

A standard fact in number theory is that if a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible over ℚ then for “almost all” primes p its reduction mod p is irreducible. (In fact, one may show that if f is irreducible over ℚ then there are infinitely many primes p for which f remains irreducible in Fₚ[x].) Hence, if f is irreducible over ℤ (and hence over ℚ) then there is some prime p for which f (mod p) is irreducible. Consequently, f is splitty (i.e. f (mod p) factors nontrivially for every prime p) if and only if f is reducible over ℤ.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. Finding all n ≤ 100 for which f factors over ℤ

Since f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n is a quartic with no x³‐ or x‑terms, the only possible nontrivial factorization over ℤ is into two quadratics. Write

  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + ax + b)(x² + cx + d),
with a, b, c, d ∈ ℤ. Expanding the product we get

  (x² + ax + b)(x² + cx + d) = x⁴ + (a + c)x³ + (ac + b + d)x² + (ad + bc)x + bd.

By comparing coefficients with x⁴ + 16x² + n we must have

1. a + c = 0            (no x³‐term)
2. ac + (b + d) = 16       (coefficient of x²)
3. ad + bc = 0           (no x‑term)
4. bd = n.

Since a + c = 0, write c = –a. Then condition (2) becomes

  –a² + (b + d) = 16   ⇒ b + d = 16 + a².

Also, condition (3) becomes

  a(d – b) = 0.
Thus we have two cases.

Case 1. a = 0.
Then c = 0 and the conditions reduce to:
  b + d = 16  and bd = n.
In other words, n is the product of two integers whose sum is 16. (Note that if f had a linear factor then f would have an integer root; but since x⁴ + 16x² is always nonnegative for integer x, an integer root would force n ≤ 0. Thus the only possibility is a factorization into quadratics.)
The pairs (b, d) of positive integers with b + d = 16 are:
  (1,15), (2,14), (3,13), (4,12), (5,11), (6,10), (7,9), (8,8).
Their products give:
  1·15 = 15, 2·14 = 28, 3·13 = 39, 4·12 = 48, 5·11 = 55, 6·10 = 60, 7·9 = 63, 8·8 = 64.
Thus from Case 1 we obtain the n–values:
  n ∈ {15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64}.

Case 2. d = b.
Then c = –a and the conditions become:
  2b – a² = 16  and b² = n.
That is, n must be a perfect square and if we write b = √n then
  2√n – a² = 16  or a² = 2√n – 16.
For a² to be nonnegative we need 2√n – 16 ≥ 0, i.e. √n ≥ 8 so n ≥ 64. Writing √n = b we have
  a² = 2b – 16.
For integer a the right‐side must be a perfect square. Write a = 2m (m ∈ ℤ); then
  (2m)² = 4m² = 2b – 16  ⇒ b = 2m² + 8.
Then n = b² = (2m² + 8)².
For n ≤ 100 we must have m = 0 or m = ±1.
• If m = 0 then b = 8 and n = 64.
• If m = 1 (or –1) then b = 2 + 8 = 10 and n = 10² = 100.
Thus from Case 2 we obtain n = 64 (again) and n = 100.

Combining the two cases, the positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f(x) factors over ℤ (and hence is splitty) are

  n ∈ {15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100}.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. Summing the values

We now add these numbers:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

───────────────────────────── 
Conclusion

The sum of all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which the polynomial x⁴ + 16x² + n is splitty is 472.

Thus, the final answer is 472.

We will show that for the quartic

  f(x) = x⁴ + 16x² + n

to be “splitty” (that is, for every prime p there exist polynomials gₚ, hₚ in ℤ[x] with deg(gₚ), deg(hₚ) < 4 such that every coefficient of f – gₚ·hₚ is divisible by p) it is necessary and sufficient that f factors nontrivially over ℤ. (In other words, f must be reducible in ℤ[x].) Here is one way to see this:

• If f factors nontrivially in ℤ[x] as a product of two polynomials of degree less than 4, then for any prime p the reduction modulo p gives a factorization of f (mod p) into two polynomials of degree less than 4. (One must check that no “accidental” cancellation makes one factor become a constant modulo p; this does not happen because the factors are monic.)

• Conversely, if f is splitty then for every prime p the polynomial f (mod p) factors as a product of two nonconstant polynomials. In particular, for “most” primes f (mod p) is reducible and one may show (using, for example, the Chebotarev density theorem) that f must then factor over ℚ and hence over ℤ.

Thus our task reduces to finding all positive integers n ≤ 100 for which

  x⁴ + 16x² + n

factors nontrivially in ℤ[x].

A natural idea is to try to factor f as a product of two quadratics. Write

  x⁴ + 16x² + n = (x² + A x + B)(x² + C x + D).

Expanding the right‐side we get

  x⁴ + (A + C)x³ + (AC + B + D)x² + (AD + BC)x + B D.

Matching coefficients with f we must have

  (1) A + C = 0,
  (2) AC + B + D = 16,
  (3) AD + BC = 0,
  (4) B D = n.

Since (1) gives C = –A, substitute this into (3):
  A·D + B·(–A) = A(D – B) = 0.
Thus either

  Case 1. A = 0  or  Case 2. D = B.

Let’s analyze these cases.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. A = 0

Then C = 0 and (2) becomes
  0 + B + D = 16 ⟹ B + D = 16.
Also, (4) tells us n = B·D.

Thus f factors as
  f(x) = (x² + B)(x² + D)
with B + D = 16 and n = B·D.

For n > 0 we need 0 < B < 16 (since if B = 0 or B = 16 then n = 0). Writing D = 16 – B, we have
  n = B(16 – B) = 16B – B² = 64 – (B – 8)².
As B runs through the integers 1, 2, …, 15, the possible values of n (ignoring repeats) are:
  B = 1: n = 64 – 49 = 15,
  B = 2: n = 64 – 36 = 28,
  B = 3: n = 64 – 25 = 39,
  B = 4: n = 64 – 16 = 48,
  B = 5: n = 64 – 9 = 55,
  B = 6: n = 64 – 4 = 60,
  B = 7: n = 64 – 1 = 63,
  B = 8: n = 64 – 0 = 64.
(The values for B = 9,…,15 repeat these numbers.) Thus from Case 1 we obtain the n‐values:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64.
──────────────────────────────
Case 2. D = B

Now (2) becomes
  A(–A) + B + B = –A² + 2B = 16 ⟹ 2B = 16 + A² ⟹ B = (16 + A²)/2.
Also, (4) gives n = B².

For B to be an integer we must have A² + 16 even. (Notice A² is even when A is even and odd when A is odd; thus A must be even.) Write A = 2k (with k ∈ ℤ). Then
  B = (16 + 4k²)/2 = 8 + 2k²  and  n = B² = (8 + 2k²)².
We now require n ≤ 100.
• For k = 0: B = 8, n = 8² = 64.
• For k = ±1: B = 8 + 2 = 10, n = 10² = 100.
• For |k| ≥ 2: n ≥ (8 + 8)² = 16² = 256, which is too large.
Thus from Case 2 we get the additional n‐value 100 (note that 64 was already obtained).

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The positive integers n ≤ 100 for which f(x) factors nontrivially in ℤ[x] (and hence is splitty) are:
  15, 28, 39, 48, 55, 60, 63, 64, 100.

The problem asks for the sum of these n‐values. Adding them we get:
  15 + 28 = 43,
  43 + 39 = 82,
  82 + 48 = 130,
  130 + 55 = 185,
  185 + 60 = 245,
  245 + 63 = 308,
  308 + 64 = 372,
  372 + 100 = 472.

Thus, the required sum is 472.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer: 472

  f(x) ≡ gₚ(x)·hₚ(x) (mod p)

  (x² + B)(x² + D) = x⁴ + (B + D)x² + BD.

  B + D = 16  and  BD = n  (in ℤ/p).
